name: Shock & Hemodynamics
sub: Shock types, fluids, vasopressors, monitoring, tamponade

cards.q: Classify shock and give an example of each type.
cards.a: Hypovolaemic (haemorrhage), cardiogenic (MI, acute heart failure), distributive (sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic), obstructive (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, massive PE).

cards.q: What is the typical haemodynamic profile of cardiogenic versus distributive shock?
cards.a: Cardiogenic: low cardiac output, high SVR, high filling pressures. Distributive: normal or high cardiac output, low SVR, low or normal filling pressures.

cards.q: Which dynamic tests predict fluid responsiveness?
cards.a: Passive leg raise with a cardiac output rise >10%; pulse pressure variation >12–13% (controlled ventilation, sinus rhythm, tidal volume ≥8 mL/kg); IVC variation (>12–18%) in ventilated patients; fluid challenge with echo velocity time integral rise.

cards.q: Why is CVP a poor guide to fluid responsiveness?
cards.a: A single static CVP value does not reliably predict preload responsiveness because venous tone, intrathoracic pressure and ventricular compliance vary; trends and dynamic indices are better.

cards.x: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign suggests at least {{c1::30 mL/kg}} of {{c2::crystalloid}} in the first {{c3::3 hours}} for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion, preferring {{c4::balanced crystalloids}} over saline.

cards.q: What is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock and the usual MAP target?
cards.a: Norepinephrine, targeting MAP 65 mmHg. Add vasopressin when the norepinephrine dose reaches about 0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min, and consider epinephrine if further support is needed.

cards.q: When is hydrocortisone added in septic shock?
cards.a: In patients with ongoing vasopressor requirement (norepinephrine or epinephrine ≥0.25 mcg/kg/min for at least 4 hours): hydrocortisone 200 mg/day, usually 50 mg IV every 6 hours.

cards.q: What was the result of SEPSISPAM on higher MAP targets?
cards.a: A MAP target of 80–85 mmHg versus 65–70 mmHg did not reduce mortality, and caused more atrial fibrillation; patients with chronic hypertension needed less renal replacement therapy.

cards.q: Give the ATLS classes of haemorrhage by percentage blood volume lost.
cards.a: Class I <15%, class II 15–30%, class III 30–40% (hypotension, tachycardia, anxiety), class IV >40% (immediately life threatening, near-collapse).

cards.q: What dose and timing apply to tranexamic acid in trauma?
cards.a: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours, started within 3 hours of injury (CRASH-2).

cards.q: Describe Beck's triad and the echo signs of cardiac tamponade.
cards.a: Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds. Echo: pericardial effusion, right atrial and early diastolic right ventricular collapse, a plethoric IVC and exaggerated respiratory variation in inflow.

cards.q: What is pulsus paradoxus and when does it occur?
cards.a: An inspiratory fall in systolic BP of more than 10 mmHg. Seen in tamponade, severe asthma or COPD, tension pneumothorax and constrictive pericarditis.

cards.x: Systemic vascular resistance is calculated as 80 × ({{c1::MAP}} − {{c2::CVP}}) ÷ {{c3::cardiac output}}, with a normal range of about {{c4::800–1200}} dyn·s/cm⁵.

cards.q: What are the normal pulmonary artery catheter values?
cards.a: RA 2–6 mmHg, RV 15–30/2–8, PA 15–30/6–12 (mean 9–18), PCWP 6–12 mmHg, cardiac index 2.5–4 L/min/m².

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment of anaphylaxis?
cards.a: Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 minutes if needed, with oxygen, IV fluids and airway support; adjuncts include antihistamines and steroids only after adrenaline.

cards.q: How do you treat neurogenic shock?
cards.a: Fluids to restore volume, then norepinephrine (or phenylephrine) to maintain MAP; treat bradycardia with atropine or an infusion; look for other causes of hypotension and for concurrent haemorrhage.

cards.q: What does a normal ScvO₂ target look like and its limitation?
cards.a: ScvO₂ above about 70% was an old resuscitation target; high values can reflect impaired oxygen extraction in sepsis, so it should be interpreted with lactate and clinical perfusion.

cards.q: How does dobutamine support a failing heart and what are its risks?
cards.a: β1 agonist increasing contractility and cardiac output (2.5–20 mcg/kg/min); β2 effect may cause vasodilation and hypotension; tachyarrhythmia and tachyphylaxis are risks.

cards.q: A patient with chest stab wound is hypotensive, JVP is raised, heart sounds are muffled and lungs are clear. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
o: Cardiac tamponade; pericardiocentesis or emergency thoracotomy
cards.e: Beck's triad indicates tamponade. Penetrating tamponade needs surgical decompression; pericardiocentesis is a temporising option.

cards.q: A septic patient remains hypotensive on norepinephrine 0.3 mcg/kg/min. What is the recommended next step?
o: Add vasopressin and consider IV hydrocortisone
Stop norepinephrine and start dobutamine alone
cards.e: SSC 2021 suggests adding vasopressin at about 0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min norepinephrine and corticosteroids for ongoing requirements.

cards.q: Which fluid is generally preferred for resuscitation in critical illness?
cards.e: Balanced crystalloids are preferred over normal saline (SMART, SALT-ED); starches increase AKI and mortality; albumin may be added when large volumes of crystalloid are needed.

cards.q: What does a positive passive leg raise test involve?
cards.a: Move the patient from a semi-recumbent position to supine with legs raised 45° (without stimulation). A rise in cardiac output or stroke volume >10% within 1–2 minutes indicates fluid responsiveness.

cards.q: What is the role of vasopressin and its effect on the splanchnic bed?
cards.a: V1 receptor agonist that restores vascular tone independent of catecholamine receptors; fixed dose 0.03 units/min; risks are digital and splanchnic ischaemia and hyponatraemia.
